source_text: XL. Postea vero monet, pro ratione donorum Dei in talibus, & excellentiae majoris vel minoris, nos etiam augere observantiae & venerationis gradus: & laudes iis debitas non aequare, sed cuique pro ea quam in eo agnoscimus mensura, tribuere quod suum est. Neminem vero qui opera nostra non habet opus, & cui non potest usui esse, nos colere servitute proprie dicta. Nec enim nos Sanctorum qui obierunt servos esse, sed ejusdem haereditatis consortes futuros, eorumque vestigia, quantum possumus, etiam premere: quod maxime voluerunt, dum in terris versantes, exemplo praeiverunt, Christum imitando, ut eos imitaremur.
english: Rivet next warns that we should raise the degrees of observance and veneration in proportion to the gifts God has given such persons and to their greater or lesser excellence. We are not to make the praises due them all equal, but to give each what is his own, according to the measure we recognize in him.
But we do not serve with servitude properly so called anyone who has no need of our works and to whom we can be of no use.
For we are not the servants of the saints who have died. We are to be sharers of the same inheritance with them, and to press on in their footsteps as far as we can.
That is what they most wanted while they lived on earth, when they went before us by example, imitating Christ so that we might imitate them.

source_text: XIII. Ut autem distinctius intelligatur quae sit de hac quaestione Doctorum Scholae Romanae sententia, visum est hic referre quae ea de re accurate & perspicue admodum tradit Gul. Estius in secundum sententiarum Distinctione 19. num. 9. Ibi enim ad quaestionem, Utrum immortalitas primi status fuerit homini naturalis, per multas & varias distinctiones Respondet. Et docet eam illi quadam ratione naturalem, & quadam ratione supra naturam fuisse; sicut & mors homini lapso quadam ratione naturalis est, quadam ratione contra naturam.
english: To make the view of the Roman school's teachers on this question clearer, I think it worth setting out what William Estius teaches on it, very precisely and clearly, in his commentary on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 19, number 9.

There he answers the question "Whether the immortality of the first state was natural to man" with many different distinctions. He teaches that it was natural to man in one respect and above nature in another, just as death is natural to fallen man in one respect and against nature in another.

source_text: XIV. Primo enim naturale dicitur quod inest a prima institutione naturae. Et hac ratione dicit immortalitatem fuisse primo homini naturalem, mortem vero contra naturam, quoniam homo initio institutus est immortalis, id est, a moriendi necessitate liber.
english: First, what is present from nature's first institution is called natural. In this sense he says that immortality was natural to the first man and death against nature, since man was created immortal at the beginning, that is, free from the necessity of dying.

source_text: XV. Item naturale dicitur id in quod naturaliter fertur cujusque appetitus. Et etiam sic concedit immortalitatem homini naturalem esse, & mortem contra naturam, quoniam omnes natura appetunt immortalitatem, mortem vero refugiunt.
english: Again, what each thing's appetite naturally tends toward is called natural. In this sense too he grants that immortality is natural to man and death against nature, because everyone by nature longs for immortality and shrinks from death.

source_text: XVI. Praeterea naturale significare potest quod cuique inest a nativitate, sive sit naturae bonum atque conveniens, & naturali appetitui consentaneum, sive non. Et ita quoque fatetur primo homini immortalitatem, mortalitatem vero nobis naturalem esse. Ille enim immortalis conditus fuit, nos autem nascimur morti obnoxii.
english: Natural can also mean what each person has from birth, whether it is good for nature, suited to it and in keeping with natural appetite, or not. In this sense too, he admits, immortality was natural to the first man and mortality is natural to us. He was created immortal; we are born subject to death.

source_text: XVII. Rursum addit naturale dici id quod in ipsa natura causam habet. Et etiam, inquit, hoc pacto immortalitas fuit primo homini quodammodo naturalis. Nam in optima humani corporis temperie tanquam interna causa, & in ligno vitae tanquam externa causa (quarum utraque ad illum effectum naturalis erat) immortalitas consistebat.
english: He adds that what has its cause in nature itself is called natural. "In this way too," he says, "immortality was in a manner natural to the first man. For it rested on the excellent balance of the human body as its inner cause and on the tree of life as its outer cause, and each of these was a natural cause of that effect."

source_text: XVIII. Caeterum docet alia ratione eandem immortalitatem homini fuisse supernaturalem: partim quidem ratione justitiae, a qua bona illa corporis constitutio, & ex consequenti immortalitas ipsa dependebat. Erat enim, inquit, illa justitia supernaturalis, quatenus per eam anima Deo subjiciebatur, & adhaerebat, ut bono ac fini suo supernaturali. Qua subjectione durante, inerat animae vis quaedam supernaturalis, per quam poterat corpus, ab omni corruptione praeservare. Partim ratione corporis, sive materiae ex qua homo factus est. Quae cum terrena fuerit, causam in se immortalitatis non habebat, sed potius mortalitatis. Quamvis igitur, inquit, primus homo in ipsa natura causam quandam habuerit immortalitatis, non tamen plenam & totalem. Quin potius si dona supernaturalia cogitatione ab eo separemus, & sola in eo consideremus naturalia, mortalis erat, ita ut necesse esset eum mori. Erat enim compositus ex contrariis, quorum pugnam necessario tandem consequitur ipsius compositi corruptio. Juxta hunc igitur modum immortalitas erat primo homini supernaturalis. Quoniam autem supernaturale proprie non opponitur ei quod primo, secundo, vel tertio modo naturale dicitur ex modis jam enumeratis, sed ei tantum quod quarto modo: secundum quem tamen non potest immortalitas primo homini dici simpliciter naturalis; quia ad eam homini praestandam solae causae naturales, uti diximus, non sufficiebant; idcirco potius absolute supernaturalis dici debet immortalitas homini integro, quam naturalis. Unde propositio illa qua dicitur immortalitatem primi hominis non fuisse gratiae beneficium, sed naturalem conditionem, merito a sede Apostolica improbata est: maxime si sensus ejus sit immortalitatem ita esse debitam naturae humanae, ut Deus non potuerit eam creare mortalem. Hoc enim constat esse falsissimum.
english: But Estius teaches that in another respect this same immortality was supernatural to man. Partly because of righteousness, on which the body's good constitution, and so immortality itself, depended. "That righteousness," he says, "was supernatural, inasmuch as through it the soul was subject to God and clung to him as its supernatural good and end. As long as that subjection lasted, the soul had a certain supernatural power by which it could keep the body from all corruption." And partly because of the body, that is, the matter from which man was made. Since that matter was earthy, it held in itself no cause of immortality, but rather of mortality.

"So although the first man," he says, "had in his very nature some cause of immortality, it was not a full and complete one. On the contrary, if in thought we set his supernatural gifts aside and consider only what was natural in him, he was mortal, so that he would have had to die. For he was made of contraries, and the dissolution of the compound necessarily follows from their conflict in the end. In this way, then, immortality was supernatural to the first man.

"But the supernatural is properly opposed not to what is called natural in the first, second or third of the senses just listed, but only to what is natural in the fourth sense. In that sense the first man's immortality cannot be called simply natural, because, as we said, natural causes alone were not enough to give it to him. So the immortality of unfallen man should be called supernatural, absolutely speaking, rather than natural.

"That is why the Apostolic See rightly condemned the proposition that the first man's immortality was not a gift of grace but a natural condition, especially if it means that immortality was so owed to human nature that God could not have created it mortal. That is clearly utterly false."

source_text: XIX. Quod spectat autem Scholae Reformatae Doctores, illi quoque communi consensu docent hominem in statu innocentiae fuisse aliquatenus immortalem. Nec etiam dissimili ratione explicant istam immortalitatem. Nam cum Doctoribus Ecclesiae Romanae, distinguunt inter immortalitatem qua aliquis non potest mori, & inter eam qua aliquis potest non mori, & est a necessitate moriendi immunis. Priori modo solos beatos post resurrectionem immortales fore docent; sed posteriori tantum hominem in statu integro fuisse immortalem; ita ut in eo esset possibilitas moriendi, quae non est in beatis, non esset vero, quae jam est in nobis per peccatum, moriendi necessitas.
english: As for the teachers of the Reformed school, they too hold by common consent that man in the state of innocence was immortal in some measure, and they explain that immortality in much the same way.

Like the teachers of the Roman Church, they distinguish the immortality by which someone is unable to die from the immortality by which someone is able not to die and is free from the necessity of dying. In the first sense, they teach, only the blessed after the resurrection will be immortal. Man in his unfallen state was immortal only in the second sense: he had the possibility of dying, which the blessed do not have, but not the necessity of dying, which we now have through sin.

source_text: XX. Hanc rem sic exponit Josue Placeus Thesibus de statu Adami ante lapsum Thesi 32. Non erat, inquit, immortalis Adamus, quomodo nos erimus post beatam resurrectionem: poterat enim, ut peccare, sic mori. Nec erat mortalis, quemadmodum nos mortales sumus in hoc statu peccati: poterat enim, ut non peccare, ita non mori.
english: Josué de la Place (Placaeus) puts it this way in thesis 32 of his Theses on the State of Adam before the Fall: "Adam's immortality was not the kind we shall have after the blessed resurrection, since he was able to sin and so able to die. Nor was his mortality the kind we have now in this state of sin, since he was able to avoid sin and so able to avoid death."

source_text: XXI. Et similiter Pareus immortalitatem illam, qua homo ante peccatum corpore immortalis erat, dicit fuisse potentiam non moriendi, seu negationem actus moriendi, ex hypothesi unionis cum anima originaliter perfecta, licet corpus hominis esset in se mortale. Immortalitas, inquit, significat primo impotentiam moriendi absolutam & natura. Sic solus Deus immortalitatem habet. Sic Patres negant, & nos negamus hominem immortalem fuisse natura. Secundo impotentiam moriendi ex gratia creationis: Sic Angeli, animae humanae sunt immortales. Tertio impotentiam moriendi ex gratia doni: sic corpora beatorum immortalitatem habebunt. Quarto potentiam non moriendi, seu negationem actus moriendi, ex aliqua hypothesi, licet in se sit mortale. Sic homo ante peccatum immortalis erat corpore, ex hypothesi unionis cum anima originaliter perfecta, immortali. In lib. adversus Bell. de Grat. primi hominis, cap. 9.
english: Pareus likewise says that the immortality by which man before sin was immortal in body was a power of not dying, that is, the absence of the act of dying, on the supposition of its union with a soul perfect from its origin, although man's body was mortal in itself.

"Immortality," he says, "means first an inability to die that is absolute and by nature. In this sense God alone has immortality, and in this sense the Fathers deny, and we deny, that man was immortal by nature. Second, an inability to die by the grace of creation: so angels and human souls are immortal. Third, an inability to die by the grace of a gift: so the bodies of the blessed will have immortality. Fourth, a power of not dying, that is, the absence of the act of dying, on some supposition, though the thing is mortal in itself. In this sense man before sin was immortal in body, on the supposition of its union with an immortal soul perfect from its origin." (Pareus, against Bellarmine, On the Grace of the First Man, chapter 9.)

source_text: XXII. Tilenus quoque Disputatione de statu externo primi hominis thesi nona. Sciendum est, inquit, immortalitatem primi hominis non plane ejusdem fuisse rationis cum gloriosa Beatorum immortalitate. Nam ut aliud est posse non peccare, & non posse peccare: sic aliud posse non mori, & non posse mori. Illud est naturae, hoc gloriae. Prior immortalitas moriendi actum tollit, potestatem non excludit: posterior utrumque abolet & extinguit.
english: Tilenus says the same in his Disputation on the External State of the First Man, ninth thesis: "It should be understood that the first man's immortality was not wholly of the same kind as the glorious immortality of the blessed. For as being able not to sin is one thing and being unable to sin another, so being able not to die is one thing and being unable to die another. The first belongs to nature, the second to glory. The first kind of immortality removes the act of dying but does not rule out the power to die; the second abolishes and extinguishes both."

source_text: XXIII. Caeterum istam immortalitatem quae homini in integritate primigenia competebat, pertendunt dici debere potius naturalem quam supernaturalem, & revera primum hominem aliquo sensu fuisse natura immortalem. Haec est doctrina Tileni Disputationis modo citatae Thesi octava. Ubi asserit hominem vere dici natura immortalem. Thesi tamen secunda mentem suam distinctius explicans, docet corpus primi hominis per se quidem fuisse corruptibile, quippe ex contrariis, & inter se pugnantibus qualitatibus conflatum: Veruntamen ex Dei pacto incorruptibile fuisse futurum, si homo in Dei obsequio constitisset sine peccato.
english: The Reformed, however, maintain that the immortality man had in his first integrity should be called natural rather than supernatural, and that the first man really was in some sense immortal by nature. This is what Tilenus teaches in the eighth thesis of the disputation just cited, where he says that man is truly called immortal by nature.

Yet in the second thesis, explaining his meaning more precisely, he teaches that the first man's body was in itself corruptible, since it was made up of contrary qualities in conflict with one another, but that by God's covenant it would have been incorruptible had man continued in obedience to God without sin.

source_text: XXIV. Sic etiam ea de re pronunciat Josue Placeus thesi jam allegata. Tam naturalis, inquit, erat Adamo facultas non moriendi, quam non peccandi. Haud magis est a natura mortis quam peccati imperium. Possibilitatem quidem moriendi a natura habuit, necessitatem vero a peccato. Cujus rei hanc rationem affert, quod aequum sit facultates Physicas sequi conditionem Moralium, penes quas est imperium in homine: Unde colligit in Adamo eandem fuisse rationem vitae & justitiae. Ac proinde cum justitia ipsi fuerit naturalis, naturalem quoque esse debuisse non moriendi facultatem.
english: Josué de la Place says the same in the thesis already cited: "The power of not dying was as natural to Adam as the power of not sinning. The reign of death is no more from nature than the reign of sin. He had the possibility of dying from nature, but the necessity of dying from sin."

He gives this reason: it is fitting that the physical powers follow the condition of the moral powers, which rule in man. From this he concludes that in Adam life and righteousness stood on the same footing, and so, since righteousness was natural to him, the power of not dying must have been natural too.

source_text: XXV. Pareus vero distinguit inter naturam integram & naturam corruptam. Et dicit Adami immortalitatem, respectu naturae integrae fuisse naturalem: respectu vero naturae corruptae, non immortalitatem, sed mortalitatem, quae est moriendi necessitas, naturalem recte dici. Ac praeterea distinguit inter hominem integrum, & corpus ejus in se consideratum. Et homini, non corpori in se, immortalitatem naturalem fuisse asserit, in caput nonum Bellarmini de gratia primi hominis. Capite vero quinto homini integro docet naturale fuisse quicquid principiis naturae, ad ejus perfectionem per se adjacebat; & sine quo natura in suis principiis non erat primitus condita.
english: Pareus distinguishes between nature unfallen and nature corrupted. He says that with respect to unfallen nature Adam's immortality was natural, but that with respect to corrupted nature it is not immortality but mortality, that is, the necessity of dying, that is rightly called natural.

He also distinguishes between unfallen man and man's body considered in itself, and holds that immortality was natural to the man, not to the body in itself (on Bellarmine, On the Grace of the First Man, chapter 9). In chapter 5 he teaches that whatever belonged of itself to the principles of nature for its perfection, and without which nature was not first made in its principles, was natural to unfallen man.

source_text: XXVI. Porro in hac quaestione illud omnino certum est, &, ut ex dictis apparet, communi consensu Scholae tam Romanae quam Reformatae probatum, hominem ante peccatum fuisse a necessitate moriendi immunem, in eo tamen fuisse, ut peccandi, sic etiam moriendi possibilitatem. Et hominem non alio quam isto sensu fuisse immortalem.
english: In this question one thing is entirely certain and, as appears from what has been said, approved by the common consent of both the Roman and the Reformed schools: before sin man was free from the necessity of dying, yet so placed that he could sin, and so could also die. And man was immortal in no other sense than this.

source_text: XXVII. Nec etiam negant Scholae Romanae Theologi, ut supra fuit a nobis ostensum, immortalitatem istam, quae primo homini ante peccatum competebat, naturalem certo respectu & sensu dici posse, nempe quatenus naturale significat quod est a prima Origine insitum, non autem adventitium atque superadditum: Item quatenus naturale opponitur ei quod est contra naturam, & significat id quod eandem naturam ornat atque perficit.
english: Nor do the theologians of the Roman school deny, as we showed above, that the immortality the first man had before sin can be called natural in a certain respect and sense. It can be so called insofar as "natural" means what was implanted from the first origin, not something added from outside and laid on top. It can also be so called insofar as "natural" is opposed to what is against nature and means what adorns and perfects that same nature.

source_text: XXVIII. Quaestio solum remanet An simpliciter loquendo immortalitas ista dici potius debeat naturalis quam supernaturalis Respectu hominis integri? Quod affirmant Protestantes, Doctores vero Scholae Romanae negant.
english: The only question left is whether, simply speaking, this immortality should be called natural rather than supernatural with respect to unfallen man. The Protestants say yes; the teachers of the Roman school say no.

source_text: XXIX. Verum quaestio ista solum est de nomine, respectu eorum qui inter Protestantes naturale cum Paraeo definiunt, Id sine quo natura in suis principiis non fuit primitus condita. Hoc enim sensu fatentur, ut vidimus, Doctores Scholae Romanae immortalitatem fuisse primo homini naturalem.
english: But for those Protestants who define "natural" with Pareus as "that without which nature was not first made in its principles," the question is only about a word. For in that sense, as we have seen, the teachers of the Roman school admit that immortality was natural to the first man.

source_text: XXX. Dissidium solum quoddam reale remanebit inter eos ex Protestantibus qui volunt, sine omni auxilio supernaturali, hominem integrum mortem in perpetuum potuisse vitare, & Scholam Romanam quae id communi consensu negat.
english: The only real disagreement left will be between those Protestants who hold that unfallen man could have escaped death forever without any supernatural help, and the Roman school, which by common consent denies it.

source_text: XXXI. Caeterum modo constet necessitatem moriendi quae jam nobis incumbit non a natura, sed a peccato esse; & si homo in primaeva integritate perstitisset, vitam cum ejus justitia semper fuisse conjungendam, ex sapientissimo & aequissimo Dei instituto, quaestio ista non videtur ita magni esse momenti.
english: Still, provided it is agreed that the necessity of dying that now lies on us comes not from nature but from sin, and that had man persevered in his original integrity, life would always have been joined to his righteousness by God's most wise and most just decree, this question does not seem very important.

source_text: XXXII. Ut distinctius tamen aperiam quis sit meus ea de re sensus. Observo in Scholis Reformatis, circa perpetuo futuram hominis integri vitam, duas esse sententias. Etenim nonnulli sunt qui censent primum hominem, si juxta naturae foedus cum ipso a Deo contractum, in obsequio Dei permansisset, perpetuo quidem victurum fuisse, sed solummodo vita terrena atque animali, quae in caelestem atque gloriosam nunquam commutanda fuisset. Quae est doctrina Mosis Amyraldi Thesibus de tribus foederibus divinis.
english: To make my own view on this clearer: I find two opinions in the Reformed schools about the unending life unfallen man would have had.

Some hold that if the first man had remained in obedience to God, according to the covenant of nature God made with him, he would indeed have lived forever, but only with an earthly, animal life that would never have been changed into a heavenly and glorious one. This is what Moses Amyraut teaches in his Theses on the Three Divine Covenants.

source_text: XXXIII. Communior vero sententia tenet, hominem si primigenia integritate nunquam excidisset, assumendum tandem fuisse ad beatam & gloriosam in caelis immortalitatem, post decursum aliquod in his terris spatium, prout sapientiae divinae visum esset. Idque per immutationem similem illi quam experientur pii & sancti homines, quos ultimum judicium in terra vivos deprehendet.
english: The more common opinion holds that if man had never fallen from his original integrity, he would at last have been taken up into a blessed and glorious immortality in heaven, after spending some span of time on this earth, as God's wisdom saw fit.
This would have happened through a change like the one the godly and holy will undergo who are found alive on earth at the last judgment.

source_text: XXXIV. Si hanc, quae communior & probabilior est, sententiam sequamur, certum est hominem nunquam perpetuo victurum fuisse absque auxilio supernaturali. Nam immutatio illa per quam homo fuisset in vitam caelestem assumptus, non fuisset naturalis, sed supernaturalis.
english: This opinion is both the more common and the more probable. On it, plainly, man could never have gone on living forever unless God helped him beyond nature, since the change that was to carry him up into heavenly life would itself have been a supernatural change, not a natural one.

source_text: XXXV. Hominem autem in aeternum vivere potuisse vita terrena atque animali, ut prior illa sententia asserit, absque ullo supernaturali dono, vel auxilio, nullo modo mihi probabile videtur. Nec enim capere possum quomodo corpus ex elementis constans, adeoque naturaliter & in se corruptibile, absque ullo supra naturam auxilio, a corruptione possit in perpetuum praeservari. Qua in re judicium sequor Petri Molinaei, cui quoque dubium non est quin, homo quantumvis perfecto corporis temperamento naturali, opus habeat auxilio supernaturali, & Dei ope continua ad servandam hanc εὐκρασίαν. De statu Innocentiae Thesi 50.
english: But that man could have lived forever an earthly, animal life without any supernatural gift or help, as the first opinion maintains, seems to me in no way probable. I cannot see how a body made of the elements, and so naturally and in itself corruptible, could be kept from corruption forever without some help above nature.

Here I follow the judgment of Pierre du Moulin, who also has no doubt that man, however perfect the natural balance of his body, needs supernatural help and God's continual aid to keep that good balance (eukrasia) (Du Moulin, On the State of Innocence, thesis 50).
